facts.title: Named After a Mineral
facts.text: Samarium is the first chemical element named after a person, but only indirectly. It takes its name from the mineral samarskite, which honors Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets, a 19th-century Russian mining official. The element was isolated in 1879 by French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, who spotted its signature using flame spectroscopy.

facts.title: World's Strongest Permanent Magnets
facts.text: Samarium-cobalt (SmCo5 and Sm2Co17) magnets are among the most powerful permanent magnets ever made. Their standout feature is an extremely high Curie temperature of around 700-800 degrees Celsius, meaning they keep their magnetism in scorching conditions where other magnets fail. This makes them essential in jet engines, military hardware, and high-temperature motors.

facts.title: A Self-Powered Neutron Sponge
facts.text: Samarium-149 is one of the most voracious neutron absorbers known, with a thermal neutron capture cross-section of about 41,000 barns. Because it builds up as a fission product inside nuclear reactors, it acts as a 'reactor poison' that quietly soaks up neutrons and slows the chain reaction. Engineers must carefully account for this 'samarium poisoning' when controlling reactor power.

facts.title: It Slowly Glows With Alpha Rays
facts.text: Natural samarium is weakly radioactive because its isotope samarium-147 makes up about 15 percent of the element and decays by emitting alpha particles. Its half-life is enormous, roughly 106 billion years, which is far longer than the current age of the universe. This slow decay is harmless but useful, as geologists use the samarium-neodymium system to date very old rocks and meteorites.

facts.title: Medicine That Hunts Bone Pain
facts.text: The radioactive isotope samarium-153, bonded to a phosphate-like molecule called EDTMP, is used as the cancer drug Quadramet. Injected into the bloodstream, it homes in on growing bone tissue and delivers beta radiation directly to painful skeletal tumors. This targeted approach eases severe bone pain in patients with metastatic cancers of the prostate, breast, and lung.

facts.title: A Chemist's Magic Reagent
facts.text: Samarium(II) iodide, written SmI2 and nicknamed 'Kagan's reagent,' is a deep blue-green solution prized by organic chemists. It is a powerful but selective single-electron reducing agent, capable of stitching carbon-carbon bonds together in delicate molecule-building reactions. Since its introduction by Henri Kagan in 1980, it has become a workhorse for synthesizing complex natural products and drug candidates.

facts.title: Spotted Through Its Spectrum
facts.text: Samarium was discovered not by holding a lump of it, but by reading rainbows of light. When de Boisbaudran heated a sample of the mineral didymium, he saw sharp new spectral lines that belonged to no known element. This use of spectroscopy, splitting light into colored bands, was a powerful detective tool that revealed several rare-earth elements hiding inside what chemists once thought were single substances.

facts.title: Switches Crystal Shape With Heat
facts.text: Pure samarium metal is silvery, fairly hard, and stable in dry air, but it is structurally restless. As it is heated it shifts between three different crystal arrangements, and it adopts a rare rhombohedral packing at room temperature that few other elements share. It melts at about 1072 degrees Celsius, on the lower side for the lanthanide family.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Like the other rare-earth elements, samarium is not made on Earth but is forged inside stars. Most of it is created by the slow and rapid neutron-capture processes (the s-process and r-process) during the late lives and violent deaths of massive stars and in neutron-star collisions. The atoms scattered into space eventually gathered into the dust and gas that built our Solar System.

facts.title: Not So Rare After All
facts.text: Despite the label 'rare earth,' samarium is more abundant in Earth's crust than familiar metals like tin or mercury, at roughly 7 to 8 parts per million. It is mined mainly from the minerals monazite and bastnasite, with major production in China. The element has no known biological role and is not used by living cells, though it shows only low toxicity in laboratory studies.
